We have mass spec: m/z 179.0946 (intensity 100). That likely is molecular ion [M+H]+? For C10H13NO2, exact mass: C10=120.000, H13=13.101, N=14.003, O2=31.989 => total 179.093. So matches. So molecular formula C10H13NO2.

We have proton NMR: peaks: 2.58 (t, J=7.4, 2H), 2.84 (t, J=7.4, 2H), 3.81 (s, 3H), aromatic 7.17 (ddd, 2H), 7.93 (ddd, 2H). So aromatic AA'BB' pattern typical of para-disubstituted benzene. Two aromatic doublets? Actually ddd but similar. So para-disubstituted benzene with two sets of equivalent protons (2 each). Substituents likely electron-withdrawing/donating causing shift difference.

We have a methoxy (3H singlet at 3.81) typical of OCH3 attached to aromatic (anisole). So likely para-methoxy phenyl.

The aliphatic chain: two triplets each 2H at 2.58 and 2.84, J 7.4, suggests -CH2-CH2- attached to something. The more downfield (2.58) maybe adjacent to aromatic? Actually benzylic CH2 appears around 2.3-2.5. So 2.58 could be benzylic CH2 attached to aromatic ring. The other CH2 (2.84) maybe adjacent to carbonyl or heteroatom (e.g., amide). Also we have a carbonyl (C=O) and NH (since formula includes N). Could be phenethyl amide? Let's think.

Possibility: p-methoxyphenethylamine? That would be C10H13NO? Wait p-methoxy phenethylamine formula C9? Let's compute: p-anisidine (4-methoxyaniline) is C7H9NO? Actually anisidine: C7H9NO? No, anisidine is C7H9NO? Wait anisidine: C7H9NO? Actually anisidine: C7H9NO? plus OCH3 adds OCH3 (CH3O) to C6H4NH2 => C7H9NO? Let's compute: C6H4 (benzene) + OCH3 (CH3O) = C7H7O? Wait: C6H4 + OCH3 = C7H7O? Actually OCH3 adds CH3O, so total C7H7O? plus NH2 adds N H2. So C7H9NO? plus O? Actually we have O from methoxy and maybe extra O? Not.

Our formula C10H13NO2 includes two oxygens: one likely methoxy O, another carbonyl O (C=O). So we have an amide (C=O) and methoxy aromatic.

Thus structure could be p-methoxy phenylacetamide? Let's test: p-methoxy phenyl (C7H7O) plus CH2-CO-NH2? Actually phenylacetamide: C8H9NO? Wait phenylacetamide: C8H9NO? plus O? Actually amide has carbonyl O, so phenylacetamide C8H9NO? Let's compute: C6H5-CH2-CO-NH2 => C8H9NO? plus O? Actually carbonyl O is included, so formula C8H9NO? plus O? Wait carbonyl O is O, so total O1. So phenylacetamide C8H9NO? Let's compute: C6H5 (C6H5) + CH2 (CH2) + CO (C O) + NH2 (N H2) => C8 H5+2+2 = H9, N1, O1. So C8H9NO. Not match.

Our formula C10H13NO2: add methoxy OCH3 to phenylacetamide gives C9? Actually add OCH3 (CH3O) to phenyl ring (para). So C8 + C1 = C9? Wait phenylacetamide C8, add OCH3 adds C1 H3 O1, total C9? Actually C8 +1 = C9, H9+3=H12, O1+1=O2, N1 unchanged. So C9H12NO2. Not match (C10H13NO2). So maybe phenylpropionamide (C9H11NO2) plus methoxy OCH3 gives C10H14NO3? Not.

Let's examine aliphatic signals: two CH2 triplets each 2H suggests -CH2-CH2- chain. The more downfield (2.58) likely benzylic CH2 attached to aromatic. The other (2.84) attached to carbonyl (CH2-CO-). So structure: p-methoxy phenyl-CH2-CH2-CO-NH? Wait carbonyl after CH2? Actually CH2-CO would be CH2 attached to carbonyl carbon (alpha to carbonyl). That CH2 appears around 2.3-2.5 for CH2-CO. But we have 2.84, a bit more downfield maybe due to adjacent to amide nitrogen? Actually CH2 attached to carbonyl (CH2-CO) is around 2.3. CH2 attached to aromatic is around 2.7. So 2.58 could be CH2-CO, 2.84 could be benzylic. But J coupling same, they are adjacent.

Thus chain: aromatic-CH2-CH2-CO-NH2? That would be phenylpropionamide (C9H11NO). Add methoxy OCH3 on aromatic para gives C10H13NO2. Yes! Let's compute: phenylpropionamide: C9H11NO? Wait phenylpropionamide: C6H5-CH2-CH2-CO-NH2. Carbons: 6 (ring) + 2 (CH2-CH2) + 1 (CO) = 9. Hydrogens: ring 5 (C6H5) + CH2 (2) + CH2 (2) + NH2 (2) = 11. N1 O1. So C9H11NO. Add methoxy OCH3 at para: adds C1 H3 O1, but also replaces a hydrogen on ring (so net +C1 H2 O1). So final C10 H13 N O2. Yes matches formula.

Thus structure: 4-methoxyphenylpropionamide (p-anisic acid amide? Actually anisic acid is p-methoxybenzoic acid. This is p-methoxyphenylpropionamide). SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)CCCN? Wait need amide: O= C N? Actually propionamide attached to aromatic: O= C N? Wait structure: p-methoxy phenyl-CH2-CH2-CO-NH2. So SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)N? Wait need CH2-CH2-CO-NH2: aromatic-CH2-CH2-CO-NH2. So aromatic carbon attached to CH2: c1ccc(cc1)CH2CH2C(=O)N. With methoxy at para: COc1ccc(cc1)?? Let's write: COc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)N? That would be aromatic-CH2-CO-NH2 (phenylacetamide). Need two CH2: COc1ccc(cc1)CCCN? Actually need CH2-CH2-CO-NH2: COc1ccc(cc1)CCCN? Wait carbonyl after second CH2: COc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)N? That is aromatic-CH2-CH2-CO-NH2? Actually COc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)N: aromatic-CH2- C(=O)N (only one CH2). So need two CH2: COc1ccc(cc1)CCC(=O)N? That would be aromatic-CH2-CH2-CH2-CO-NH2 (propyl). Not correct.

Our chain is -CH2-CH2-CO-NH2 (two CH2 then carbonyl). So SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)N? Wait that is CH2-CO, only one CH2. So need CH2-CH2-CO: COc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)N? Actually the carbonyl carbon is attached to CH2 (alpha) and N. So CH2-CO is correct. But we need CH2-CH2-CO: aromatic-CH2-CH2-CO-NH2. So SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)N? Let's parse: aromatic carbon attached to CH2 (C), then another C attached to carbonyl? In SMILES, "CC(=O)N" is CH3-CO-NH2. For CH2-CH2-CO-NH2, we need "CCC(=O)N". So aromatic-CH2-CH2-CO-NH2 would be "COc1ccc(cc1)CC C(=O)N"? Actually "COc1ccc(cc1)CC C(=O)N" with three C's after aromatic: first CH2 attached to ring, second CH2, then carbonyl carbon. So "COc1ccc(cc1)CC C(=O)N" but need no space: "COc1ccc(cc1)CCC(=O)N". That is phenylpropionamide with methoxy para? Let's check: COc1ccc(cc1)CCC(=O)N is p-methoxy phenylpropionamide? The methoxy is attached to aromatic at position 1 (CO-). The aromatic pattern: COc1ccc(cc1) means methoxy attached to aromatic carbon at position 1, and the rest is phenyl. The chain attaches at the same carbon? Actually the SMILES attaches the chain to the aromatic after the ring closure: "COc1ccc(cc1)CCC(=O)N". The chain attaches to the aromatic at the position after the ring closure (the last aromatic carbon). In this SMILES, the chain is attached to the aromatic carbon at position 1 (the same as methoxy? Actually the ring is "c1ccc(cc1)" which is phenyl with unspecified substitution at the first carbon (where we start). The preceding "CO" attaches to that carbon (methoxy). After the ring, we have "CCC(=O)N" attached to the same carbon? In SMILES, "c1ccc(cc1)C" attaches to the aromatic carbon after the ring closure (the same as the first carbon). So we would have both methoxy and propionamide on same carbon, which is not correct. Need para substitution: methoxy at para, chain at para relative. So need to specify positions: e.g., "COc1ccc(cc1)CC C(=O)N"? Actually we need two substituents on ring: methoxy and propionamide at para positions. SMILES: "COc1ccc(cc1)CCC(=O)N" attaches propionamide at the same carbon as methoxy? Let's think: The ring is defined as "c1ccc(cc1)" which is a phenyl with two unspecified positions: the first carbon (where we start) and the last carbon (where we close). The substituents are attached to the atoms where we have external bonds. In "COc1ccc(cc1)CCC(=O)N", the "CO" attaches to the first aromatic carbon (position 1). The "CCC(=O)N" attaches to the aromatic carbon after the ring closure, which is the same as the first carbon? Actually after "c1ccc(cc1)" the default attachment is to the aromatic carbon that closed the ring (the last "c" before the "1"? The pattern "c1ccc(cc1)" has 6 aromatic atoms: positions 1-6. The SMILES string after the ring closure attaches to the aromatic atom that was just written before the closure, which is the last "c". That is position 1? Let's test: typical para-substituted anisole: "COc1ccc(cc1)C" would be anisole with methyl at para? Actually anisole is "COc1ccc(cc1)". That's methoxy attached to aromatic, no other substituent. To add a para substituent, you need to specify positions: "COc1ccc(cc1)C" attaches methyl at the same carbon as methoxy? Not correct. Real para-methoxy toluene (p-anisole) is "COc1ccc(cc1)C". Wait p-anisole is methoxy and methyl para to each other. The SMILES "COc1ccc(cc1)C" indeed represents p-anisole (para-methoxy toluene). So the pattern works: first "CO" attaches to aromatic carbon 1, then after the ring we have "C" attached to aromatic carbon 4 (para). So the SMILES attaches substituents at positions 1 and 4 automatically due to aromatic ring representation. So "COc1ccc(cc1)CCC(=O)N" would be para-methoxy phenylpropionamide. Good.

Thus candidate SMILES: "COc1ccc(cc1)CCC(=O)N". Let's validate formula: compute: aromatic C6H4 (since two substituents replace two H). Add methoxy OCH3 (C1H3O1). Add propionamide chain: -CH2-CH2-CO-NH2 adds C3 H5 N1 O1? Let's compute: CH2-CH2-CO-NH2: C3 (two CH2 + carbonyl C) H2+2+2? Wait NH2 adds 2 H. So total H: CH2 (2) + CH2 (2) + NH2 (2) =6. But carbonyl carbon has no H. So chain adds C3 H6 N1 O1. Combined with aromatic C6 H4 gives C9 H10? Wait plus methoxy C1 H3 O1 gives total C10 H13 N1 O2. Yes matches.

Now we need to verify NMR: aromatic protons: para-disubstituted benzene gives AA'BB' pattern: two doublets each 2H. Here we have ddd but okay. Chemical shifts: electron-donating methoxy shifts ortho protons upfield (~6.8) and meta ~7.2? Actually anisole protons appear around 6.9-7.2. Our observed aromatic at 7.17 and 7.93 (downfield). The 7.93 is quite downfield maybe due to electron-withdrawing amide? The amide is meta to those protons? Actually para substituents: methoxy (EDG) and propionamide (EWG). The combination leads to deshielding of protons ortho to amide (downfield). So plausible.

Aliphatic: CH2 adjacent to aromatic (benzylic) appears around 2.7-2.8 (our 2.84). CH2 adjacent to carbonyl appears around 2.5 (our 2.58). Good.

Methoxy singlet at 3.81 typical.

Thus SMILES likely correct.

We could also simulate spectra to confirm but not needed.
